match: Add support for a new environment variable that configures or extends how an existing tool, script or service behaves, keeping today's behaviour when it is unset

fit.q: Does the request add support for a new environment variable?
Does the new environment variable change or extend how an existing tool, script or service behaves?

requires.q: Does the request rename, replace or remove an environment variable that the tool already reads?

escalate.q: Does the behaviour the new variable controls get decided in several places or code paths inside the tool, rather than by one setting read in one place?

var.q: Which candidate is the name of the new environment variable, exactly as it should be spelled?

value.q: Which candidate is a literal value that the request itself writes for the new environment variable to be set to, such as a number, word or path given next to its name? Answer none if the request gives no literal value.

items.text: Add support for a new environment variable, `{var}`, keeping today's behaviour exactly when it is unset.
Make `{target_name}` read `{var}` so that it {desired}.
`{target_path}`: {target_summary}. It does not read `{var}` today.
`{target_path}`: {target_summary}. The text `{var}` already appears in it; find out what it does today before adding anything, and stop and ask if it is already read as a variable.
With `{var}` unset, output, exit codes and side effects are exactly today's; the variable changes nothing until someone sets it.
Setting `{var}` to a valid value changes only the behaviour the request describes for it; every other behaviour stays as today.
Setting `{var}` to a valid value makes `{target_name}` {desired}.
Before editing, find where the behaviour that `{var}` controls is decided today (the constant, default value or argument that sets it) and list every code path that uses that value.
Start that search by reading `{target_path}` end to end.
Write down the value the code uses today for this behaviour before editing; that value is the default when `{var}` is unset, so the unset path reproduces current behaviour exactly.
Find how `{target_name}` already reads its other environment variables (a settings loader, a naming prefix, a defaults block) and add `{var}` the same way, in the same place.

guards.q: Does `target.usage` mention environment variables that the tool already reads?

items.text: Read `{var}` once, where the tool sets up its other settings (next to argument parsing or the defaults), into one internal value that the rest of the code uses; do not read the environment again at each use.

guards.q: Does `target.usage` mention environment variables that the tool already reads?

items.text: Settle the precedence before editing and write it in a comment next to where `{var}` is read: an explicit command-line option wins over `{var}`, `{var}` wins over a config-file value, and the built-in default applies last. Keep the existing order between the other sources unchanged.

guards.q: Does `target.usage` list a command-line option or config-file key that sets the same behaviour the new variable controls?

items.text: Choose one parsing rule and commit to it: which values are valid, how a value is normalised (surrounding whitespace, letter case), and what happens on an invalid value. Criterion: an invalid value is never silently treated as a different valid one.

guards.q: Does the new variable take a value with a restricted form, such as a number, a path, or one of a fixed set of words?

items.text: With `{var}` set to a valid value, `{target_name}` {desired}.
With `{var}` unset, the stdout, stderr, exit codes and side effects of `{target_name}` are identical to today's.
`{var}` set to the empty string behaves exactly like `{var}` unset.

guards.q: Would an empty value for the new variable be meaningless, so that it can safely be treated the same as unset?

items.text: `{var}` is read when the service starts; changing it takes effect after a restart, and the documentation says so.

guards.q: Does `target.usage` describe a server or daemon that keeps running and listening until it is stopped?

items.text: An invalid value makes `{target_name}` print one error line on stderr naming `{var}`, the rejected value and what is accepted, and exit non-zero before doing any work.

items.text: An invalid value makes `{target_name}` print one error line on stderr naming `{var}` and what is accepted, without the value itself, and exit non-zero before doing any work.

items.text: `{var}` accepts a documented fixed set of on and off values (for example `1`/`true`/`yes` and `0`/`false`/`no`, case-insensitive), matching the tool's existing switches if it has any; any other value is rejected as invalid, not treated as off.

guards.q: Is the new variable an on/off switch that turns a behaviour on or off?

items.text: A non-numeric, negative or out-of-range `{var}` is rejected as invalid, and the unit (for example seconds, bytes or a count) is stated wherever `{var}` is documented.

guards.q: Does the new variable hold a number, such as a timeout, size, count or limit?

items.text: `{var}` is documented where the project documents its other configuration (help text, README or docs page) with its name, accepted values, the default when unset, and one example.
`{var}` is listed in the usage/help text of `{target_name}` in the existing format, with its default.

guards.q: Does `target.usage` include usage or help text that lists the tool's options or settings?

items.output: stdout, stderr and the exit code are identical to the same run before the change
items.reasoning: Every existing user has the variable unset; the new setting must cost them nothing.

items.input: the same run with `{var}` set to a valid value
items.output: `{target_name}` {desired}; nothing else about the run changes
items.reasoning: The variable changes only the behaviour it names, so its effect can be reasoned about in isolation.

items.input: the same run with `{var}` set to a value outside the accepted set
items.output: one stderr line naming `{var}`, the rejected value and the accepted values; non-zero exit; no work done
items.reasoning: Silently falling back to the default hides typos in the environment, which are hard to spot because nothing on the command line shows them.
